metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
Structural weight capacity, not electrical capacity, is now the binding constraint that stops AI hardware from being installed in the most retrofit data centers.

Liquid-cooled AI racks, with their coolant loops, manifolds, and battery systems, are substantially heavier than the enterprise racks most existing floors were designed to hold. The gap between the structural weight a raised floor or slab can support per square foot and the actual weight of modern AI racks is where retrofit projects stall. The data notes that structural limits are hit before electrical ones more often than the industry expected, which inverts the assumption that power delivery is always the first barrier.

This matters because it constrains where dense AI compute can physically be placed. A building may have adequate power and cooling infrastructure and still be unable to host high-density AI racks without structural reinforcement or reconstruction. That work takes time and money that are not captured in power or space metrics alone.

The data covers the definition and operational significance of floor loading limits within the category of capacity and server use. It does not provide specific load figures, failure rates, or cost estimates for remediation, so the scale of the problem across the industry cannot be derived from it. The sibling metrics, stranded power and space per cabinet, and server utilization rate, suggest the broader context is about capacity that exists on paper but cannot be fully used in practice.

siblings.label: Stranded power and space per cabinet
